Craig

Sorry for the delay. There are definitely some problems in 'secr' when addTelemetry() is applied to polygon data (strictly polygonX in the original study, I think), and the short-term solution is to discretize the capthist data:

CH <- discretize(CAPTHIST21)  # default 5-m pixels; fitting will be slow!
TeleCH <- addTelemetry(CH, Telemetry11, type = 'independent')
fit.ms <- secr.fit(TeleCH, detectfn = 'HHN' , trace = FALSE, verify = FALSE, mask = NULL)

However, I think this is a classic illustration of why one should not use telemetry data. Independent telemtry data contribute information only about sigma-hat, and even if sigma is known with certainty (and fixed in secr.fit) there is only a trivial change in the precision of D-hat. Fitting the capture + telemetry model failed for me with the data as they stand. I think the problem is that the telemetry data are centred elsewhere, outside the mask automatically generated by secr.fit(). Note also that the telemetry data (only 3 animals in the example you sent) require a very different sigma (as shown by RPSV) and are probably not applicable to the other dataset.

To fix the mask issue you can either construct a composite mask manually
telemmask <- make.mask(traps = do.call(rbind,telemetryxy(TeleCH)), spacing = 7.5, type = 'trapbuffer')
CHmask <- make.mask(traps=traps(TeleCH), spacing = 7.5, type = 'trapbuffer')
msk <- rbind(telemmask, CHmask)
or centre the telemetry data on the other survey area
centrexy <- function (xy) {
    mn <- apply(xy,2,mean) - apply(traps(CH),2,mean)
    xy <- sweep(xy, MAR=2, FUN='-', STATS = mn)
    xy
}
tmp <- telemetryxy(TeleCH)
telemetryxy(TeleCH) <- lapply(tmp, centrexy)

messages.subject_clean: Stratified sampling with detection clusters
messages.body_plain:
Hi Joe,

Not sure I follow. If you pool data from different habitat types into a single session, and do not explicitly model spatial variation in detectability or density among (individuals occupying) different habitat types, then estimates of D, g0, and sigma do not all come from data collected within the clusters, they come from the complete data set (regardless of whether any animals are detected at > 1 cluster). In this case, I think, any areas/habitat types sampled more intensively than others will have a disproportionately large influence on parameter estimates.

If you use only habitat type- or cluster-specific data to estimate habitat type-specific or cluster-specific g0, sigma, and D, then I don't see any risk of bias, but estimates might be imprecise. As soon as you combine data without adding parameters to your model, you're entering into the bias-precision trade-off. The theoretical reason to not pool data is to avoid possible bias.

That's not to say sessions are the only solution. A spatial covariate would allow you to avoid assuming constant density in a single-session analysis, and you could model differences in g0 and sigma among individuals in different habitat types using groups. Individual covariates could also be used for detectability, but aren't compatible with a spatial model of D.

Hopefully others will chime in.

Eric

Hi Solani,

My suspicion is that your issue lies with the changes that occurred during the development of SECR 4.0 (vignette found here: https://www.otago.ac.nz/density/pdfs/secr-version4.pdf ). There were several changes during this version update, many of which were aimed at improving the processing speeds of model fitting. In versions 4.0 and later, data is automatically compressed in two ways, one of which specifies that "Binary data for a particular animal and detector over s occasions are summed and modeled as a binomial count of size s on a single occasion".

Dr. Efford may be able to shed further light on the error you're experiencing, but I think your issue may have something to do with the initial reduce step you have taken, it may no longer be necessary? If you haven't already, perhaps read the SECR 4.0 vignette and you may be able to adjust your code accordingly to provide a solution. More specifically, if you set "details = list(fastproximity = FALSE)" this will be closer to fitting the models as in version 3.2, so maybe give that a go.

Anyways, I'm certainly not an expert but these are some of the things that I have tried with success when using versions 4.0 and later. Hopefully that helps.

Rory

Hmmm...

I assume you are constructing each session-specific mask and combing as a list. I get these results for an analogous example:
library(secr)
CH <- subset(ovenCHp, session = 1:2)

msk <- make.mask(traps(CH), buffer = 300, nx = 20)
fit <- secr.fit(CH, model = D~session, mask = msk)
region.N(fit)
# OK

msk <- list(make.mask(traps(CH[[1]]), buffer = 300, nx = 20),
            make.mask(traps(CH[[2]]), buffer = 300, nx = 20))
fit <- secr.fit(CH, model = D~session, mask = msk)
region.N(fit)
# error in getcellsize(mask) : mask lacks valid cell size (area or spacing)

msk <- list('2005' = make.mask(traps(CH[[1]]), buffer = 300, nx = 20),
            '2006' = make.mask(traps(CH[[2]]), buffer = 300, nx = 20))
fit <- secr.fit(CH, model = D~session, mask = msk)
region.N(fit)
# OK

So it seems region.N is unduly sensitive to the lack of names, but there is an easy workaround. The last example still has the problem that the list would not be recognised as a multi-session mask for plot, summary etc. But that would be easily fixed by setting class(msk) = c('mask','list').

Murray

I think Rory is right, with these additional notes
- fastproximity = TRUE (compression of binary proximity data to single-occasion count proximity data) is the default EXCEPT when the model does not allow it, and g0~b is one case
